title: the bell jar - sylvia plath
body:
preface

hiiiiiiii i have decided no time is better than right now to reacquaint myself with reading. it really does feel like the natural evolution of everything that interests me currently. 

im starting with the bell jar because A it is critically acclaimed B i own it C i did not fully read it when i bought it 3 years ago

i do not know much about this book, from what i remember it is about a woman who goes to school in new york and her experience with that life? i know it is a sorrowful book. the cover itself fills me with so much dread.

i think the way im going to operate this is similar to evangelion, ill write notes down during a chapter, and after each chapter ill do a small recap of everything that i know. gonna start reading now!

**chapter 1**

"the summer they electrocuted the rosenbergs"
-a couple convicted of being soviet spies, executed by electric chair
-1953

"i couldnt help wondering what it would be like, being burned alive along all your nerves"

dislikes new york, describes it similarly to how one would describe hell

buddy willard (fictional) showed narrator a cadaver that burned an image into her mind at some point in life, she compares the talk of the rosenburgs to how the cadaver haunted her

"Only I wasn't steering anything, not even myself."

she won a fashion magazine contest along with 11 other girls who were all flown out to new york to essentially be dunked into the high end fashion culture for free

she describes the makeup kit they gave her, made tailored for her, as a kit for a person with brown eyes and brown hair. she doesnt say my brown eyes and my brown hair. just a person. devaluation of herself?

the narrator is recounting her own events from this month, she has a child now. she also says she hid the things she was gifted for a while, foreshadowing bad memories associated with this time

there is a weird dynamic of the narrator both viewing herself as above the girls who lived at this hotel with her, while also being jealous of them

im almost immediately picking up on this sense of doreen being the antithesis of the narrator similar to asuka/rei. doreen is fully happy and living in the material world, while the narrator is in a completely different headspace, though she wants to be able to come back down to the material world i believe

"i always had a terribly hard time trying to imagine people in bed together"
-asexual?

"Doreen had intuition. Everything she said was like a secret voice speaking straight out of my own bones."
-gonna watch how doreen develops very carefully

"being with Doreen made me forget my worries. I felt wise and cynical as all hell"
-she wants to be doreen or she is in love with doreen?

narrator has described the last 2 men both having something to do with the color blue. maybe coincidence but figure id put it down so i remember if it happens again

Buddy Willard was a medical student at the college narrator attended

"my dream was someday ordering a drink and finding out it tasted wonderful"
-seemingly insignificant but i think this shows some lack of agency, why else point it out? actually, as a i type this, i think its more that she's so hyper-aware of herself that she won't even ask what a good drink is, she thinks that will embarrass her so instead she suffers and gambles on what she drinks. 

she describes another man as wearing blue!, the short friend of frankie

"even when they surprised me or made me sick I never let on, but pretended that's the way I knew things were all the time."

post chapter:

the narrator (who we still dont know the name of, ill call her elly for now) seems to have the worst case of scared-of-being-acknowledged-ism that i have ever witnessed. i get her though. i think i very much used to experience similar. she gives a fake name to frankie, she doesnt outwardly express her feelings, shes ashamed of where she came from, she admits to pretending she always knew things even if she just learned them.

as i typed the above I also realized the reason we may not know her name yet is because she views herself as so unimportant and is so terrified of being recognized that she won't even admit to something as menial as that in her own story.

there's obviously some connection between elly and doreen, doreen is the outgoing, confident, present girl that elly wishes she could be; doreen does not despise this difference though, elly even says she was singled out. doreen may just see a good friend in elly, while elly thinks shes being picked as a charity case

**chapter 2**

the chapter starts with frankie doreen and narrator at frankies house, he puts on some music which the author notably includes the lyric "to a true-blue gal who promised she would wait"
blue blue blue why are we so blue

doreens guy is lenny not frankie, disregard my misnaming in a few lines above

"i felt myself shrinking to a small black dot against all those red and white rugs and that pine paneling. I felt like a hole in the ground"
i feel like sylvia plath has already done such a great job of describing the feeling of being out of place or, im not exactly sure how to turn that feeling into words either. i guess thats what makes the writing special! its a very specific feeling that i very much relate to yet i dont think i could properly convey

"The silence depressed me. It wasn't the silence of silence. It was my own silence."
fully de-realizing in her room

she keeps letting out small details about Buddy Willard, now it seems his mom was trying to set them up for marriage. Buddy and his mom were both confused as to why she chose to go to New York instead

She keeps describing better and better things about Buddy. Now she's saying he's carrying the cure to Tuberculosis. I think this is turning into "hes perfect on paper, yet i still dont want to be with him. whats wrong with *me* for not wanting that?"

"I meditate in the bath... I never feel so much myself as when I'm in a hot bath"
-detachment from the material world, like her awareness is a very, very different person from the life she is living.

"Elly... the first voice mumbled, while the other voice went on hissing 'Miss Greenwood'... as if i had a split personality or something"
-thinking emoji

"I made a decision about Doreen that night. I decided I would watch her and listen to what she said, but deep down I would have nothing at all to do with her. Deep down, I would be loyal to Betsy and her innocent friends. It was Betsy I resembled at heart"

post chapter:

hmmmmmmmmmmmmmm

i had to go back to chapter 1 to figure out who Betsy was, it was the girl who invited the narrator, but not Doreen, to the party. I think it's implied in that scene that Betsy does not like Doreen, and that Betsy is trying to "save" the narrator from her. I also don't think its coincidental that Doreen is the only black character that we are aware of. i mean, this is the 50s. im confused by the line "It was Betsy I resembled at heart". to me, that almost reads as "im not good enough to be 'myself', instead I will be the Perfect Girl. Stereotypical, weary of adventure, whatever" 

i dont think she means what she said about Doreen, unless I read their relationship wrong in the first chapter

theres also this consistent theme of the narrator being left out of thing, or feeling alienated. some of that does seem to be her inability to advocate for herself though. she sees Doreen getting the things that she wants and assumes it must be because of some inherent value, meanwhile if the narrator were to speak and behave like Doreen, her life would look very different. 

**chapter 3**

"Doreen was spending the day with Lenny Shepherd. She spent most of her free time with Lenny Shepherd now." 
-notably, narrator saves doreen's keepsakes to give to her, which contradicts what she said at the end of chapter 2

"my grandmother... had the habit of saying, the minute you lifted the first forkful to your mouth, 'I hope you enjoy that, it cost forty-one cents a pound'"
-this insight into her childhood is very weighty, i can feel the foundations of the way she feels now just from this one, offhand, quote

"It was a joke because I never intended to get married"
-loaded ass page

"I wondered why I couldn't go the whole way doing what I should any more. This made me sad and tired. Then I wondered why I couldn't go the whole way doing what I shouldn't, the way Doreen did, and this made me even sadder and more tired."

ESTHER

we got her name, Jay Cee says it finally. worth nothing, the first time we learn her name is when shes being talked to in a negative sense

"What do you ahve in mind after you graduate?"
"'I don't really know,' I heard myself say. I felt a deep shock, hearing myself say that, because the minute I said it, I knew it was true"
-just in complete denial of her actual self, only going off of what others have told her is the "correct" path. shes literally shinji

"It sounded true, and I recognized it, the way you recognize some nondescript person that's been hanging around yuor door for ages and then suddenly comes up and introduces himself as your real father and looks exactly like you, so you know he really is your father, and the person you thought all your life was your father is a sham"
-she just keeps dropping these majorly significant details as if they are completely unnotable. the average person does not relate to this LOL, she refuses to acknowledge anything about herself that is 'abnormal',. or maybe she doesnt even recognize that she is 'abnormal'. i hope these notes arent coming off as critical of the character, im on her side

"I'd been telling people I'd always wanted to learn German for about five years"
-real

"my german-speaking father, dead since I was nine"

"each time i picked up a German dictionary or a German book, the very sight of those dense, black, barbed-wire letters made my mind shut like a clam."

post chapter:

a lot of character information revealed in this chapter. she speaks on a time in college where she was required to take physics and chemistry. physics, she absolutely hated, yet she was the only one in her class to get straight a's. she then applies this logic to her chemistry class, she hated it, she knows she'll get straight A's. why take it? i'm trying to think of what this says about her character. its not immediately registering for me. 

it's like she is fully capable, and knows she is fully capable, of being the "perfect" member of society, yet the idea of being that person is abhorrent. instead of acting on this and doing her own thing though, she still follows all of the guidelines, just in the least painful way for her own sake. she will inconvenience herself before she breaks any societal norms. shes stuck in a box of her own making.

it's also definitely worth noting that this is a young girl in the 50's. did she really have the choice to be who she truly wanted to be? i'm definitely catching myself over and over viewing this story through a modern lens, but if i were transported to the 50s, not even as a girl, i dont know that I would be the same person that I am right now.
